numerical_calibration.reason: Approved for riparian design and planning only. The source widths and analysis extents do not establish a shared relationship between site distance to water and buffer establishment.

retained_source_profiles.source_lineage: Forest Service and NRCS three-zone models described by Schultz et al.
retained_source_profiles.applicability: The Iowa demonstration used a separate 20 m design. Its planted treatment is not the source of the three model widths.
retained_source_profiles.locator: PDF p. 23, discussion of Forest Service and NRCS models; compare the authors’ demonstration on PDF p. 1.
retained_source_profiles.source_quote: The Forest Service and NRCS riparian forest buffer models consist of three zones of management. Zone 1 is the tree (and/or shrub) strip immediately adjacent to the stream edge that is not managed except for the occasional removal of valUable tree species. Its minimal width is ~4.6 m. Zone 2 is a managed strip of trees or shrubs extending another 18.3 m (minimum width) upland, beyond zone 1. This zone is managed for nutrient removal to stimulate efficacy of nutrient uptake. Finally, Zone 3 is a managed strip of grasses and/or forbs with a minimum width of 6.1 m selected to slow surface runoff and convert it to sheet flow.

published_profile.role: Three successive management zones for a riparian forest buffer
published_profile.interpretation: The near-stream woody strip has an approximate minimum width. The managed woody strip extends upland from its edge; the outer grass/forb strip slows surface runoff. Widths describe successive zone components.

retained_source_profiles.disposition: Keep the three successive design zones and their cited Forest Service/NRCS lineage apart from the Iowa demonstration.

retained_source_profiles.source_lineage: Tiwari et al. specified the footprint for their calculations, citing field observations of Kuglerová et al. (2014b).
retained_source_profiles.applicability: The existing planted-family link preserves review traceability. The source treats retained forest, providing a planning referral only and no evidence of planted-buffer establishment.
retained_source_profiles.locator: PDF p. 5, calculations and Figure 2, groundwater-discharge hotspot approximation.
retained_source_profiles.source_quote: In our calculations we deﬁned the groundwater discharge hotspots to extend as far as 30 m from the perennial stream with a width of 10 m along the intermittent stream (Figure 2). In reality, they could be laterally and longitudinally both wider and narrower, but ﬁeld observations conﬁrmed that 30x10 m covers their usual extent

published_profile.role: Approximate groundwater-discharge hotspot geometry for a retained-forest buffer cost comparison
published_profile.interpretation: The dimensions run on different axes. Actual hotspots can be wider or narrower in both directions. Apply a site-specific hydrological assessment if the actual footprint is needed.

retained_source_profiles.disposition: Keep both dimensions of the approximate groundwater-hotspot geometry for retained forest. The existing planted-family association confers no evidence for planting.

retained_source_profiles.source_lineage: Cole et al. cite Schmitt et al. (1999) for these two widths.
retained_source_profiles.applicability: Implementation design by pollutant target. These widths do not set distance-to-water limits.
retained_source_profiles.locator: PDF p. 3, §2.1, pollutant trapping and width.
retained_source_profiles.source_quote: Schmitt et al. (1999) suggested widths of 7.5 m are ef-fective at trapping sediments and sediment-bound pollutants (e.g. non-soluble phosphates), whereas to control soluble pollutants (e.g. nitrates and dissolved phosphorus) widths of 15 m are recommended.

published_profile.interpretation: Retain the sediment and sediment-bound pollutant strip width separately from the width recommended for soluble pollutants. Performance also depends on slope, soil and vegetation; evidence on width responses varies.

retained_source_profiles.disposition: Keep the separate pollutant-specific design widths and attribution to Schmitt et al. (1999).

numerical_calibration.source_count_basis: Three source publications documenting design or planning. No graded response or source weight is inferred.

justification: Approved for riparian design and planning only. The source widths and analysis extents do not establish a shared relationship between site distance to water and buffer establishment. Retained approved calibration hold; no new numeric synthesis or approval.
